title: Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta and 22 others sign letter against premature open-weight AI restrictions
subtitle: The 'Open Weights and American AI Leadership' coalition targets a distillation clause in draft federal AI legislation, arguing closed-only would concentrate risk.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: A coalition of 25 organizations published an open letter on July 24 titled 'Open Weights and American AI Leadership,' urging U.S. policymakers to avoid what they called premature restrictions on open-weight AI models. Signatories include Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, IBM, Dell Technologies, CrowdStrike, Palantir, ServiceNow, Hugging Face, Perplexity, Mistral, Andreessen Horowitz, Y Combinator, the Linux Foundation and Mozilla. OpenAI and Anthropic did not sign. The letter targets a distillation clause in draft federal AI legislation that would let regulators restrict training on outputs of closed models.

The substantive argument is not about openness in the abstract — it is about concentration. The signatories wrote that 'relying solely on closed models is not inherently safe: they can be breached, misused, or fail in ways that outsiders cannot detect,' and that 'concentrating advanced AI capabilities behind a small number of closed models compounds that risk.' The distillation clause is the specific policy fight — the coalition wants targeted legal frameworks for unlawful distillation instead of broad restrictions on the technique itself, which underpins how most open-weight competitors close the gap on frontier closed models.

The signatory list matters as much as the argument. Nvidia sells to everyone and has been publicly cautious about picking sides in the open-versus-closed debate; its name at the top signals that the chip market believes open-weight demand is now large enough to defend politically. Meta, whose Muse Spark 1.1 launched on July 9 as a paid API rather than open weights, still signed — hedging its bets. The absent signatures are just as loud: OpenAI and Anthropic, both preparing IPOs, have every reason to prefer a regulatory regime that treats their weights as trade secrets and treats distillation as theft.

For learners: when you read AI policy news, look at who is signing and who is not. Coalition letters are cheap to sign, so absence is more informative than presence. The Nvidia–Meta–Microsoft alignment on open weights and the OpenAI–Anthropic absence tells you the industry is now split into two structural camps — chip and platform companies whose economics depend on many models running everywhere, and frontier labs whose economics depend on a small number of models running only on their infrastructure. Every future regulation fight will fall along that same line.
